entry.title: Claims, Designs, and Guarantees: A Critical Narrative Review of Statistical Inference Reform and Practice, 2016–2026

link.title: Claims, Designs, and Guarantees: A Critical Narrative Review of Statistical Inference Reform and Practice, 2016–2026

entry.content:
Statistics helps scientists decide what their data show, but its most familiar tool, the $p$-value, is widely misunderstood. Between 2016 and 2026, professional bodies issued new guidance, and researchers developed or popularised alternatives and complements: compatibility intervals, equivalence tests, Bayes factors, and e-values that remain valid when data are checked repeatedly. Reporting rules for trials and reviews were also rewritten. Yet practice has changed little: in the biomedical literature, about 96\% of papers that report $p$-values still include at least one below 0.05. This review argues that much of the confusion comes from treating these numbers as interchangeable. Each inferential procedure carries an intended interpretation and, where applicable, a formal guarantee, such as a 5\% false-alarm rate, that holds only if the study was run and analysed in a particular way. We call this the Claim–Design–Guarantee framework: a result licenses a claim only when the claim, the design (assignment, sampling, monitoring, selection, and analysis), and the guarantee of the method are aligned. We trace the main developments of the decade, explain each tool in plain terms with formal details in boxes, and show with reproducible examples when the choice of tool changes the conclusion. For example, in a simulated two-group study with 100 interim looks, repeatedly applying an unadjusted $p<0.05$ rule produced false positives in 37.6\% of studies, whereas the particular anytime-valid e-value procedure we used produced 2.2\%, below its theoretical 5\% upper bound. We end with a decision tree, a method-selection table, and a step-by-step workflow linked to current reporting guidelines.

Read more

entry.title: Closed forms all the way up: the sample variance of four observations

link.title: Closed forms all the way up: the sample variance of four observations

entry.content:
The distribution function $F(y)=\Pr(S^2\le y)$ of the sample variance $S^2$ of four independent observations is elementary on its entire support for every polynomial parent density on $[0,1]$ (without loss of generality), and we give it in finite closed form for the uniform, Beta$(2,1)$ and Beta$(2,2)$ parents. The support splits at $y = 1/6$, $2/9$ and $1/4$, with the ceiling at $1/3$, all fixed by geometry: in coordinates aligned with the cube diagonal the event $S^2\le y$ is a ball of radius $\sqrt{3y}$, the cube projects to a rhombic dodecahedron, and these are the levels at which the ball reaches its faces, edges and two kinds of vertices. The divergence theorem reduces every moment of the clipped ball to integrals along circular arcs, so each regime closes in algebraic functions of $\sqrt{y}$ and inverse trigonometric functions. For the uniform parent the only non-obvious constant is $K_g = 12\sqrt2\arctan\sqrt2$, proportional to the mean width of the cuboctahedron; the Beta constants are rational expressions in $\pi$, $\sqrt2$, $\sqrt3$ and $\arctan\sqrt2$, as in the uniform case. At $n = 4$ the normal-theory $\chi^2$ recipe used in acceptance testing misplaces the $99$th percentile of $S^2$ by $50\%$ for the uniform parent. For three observations, polynomial parents also give elementary closed forms (arXiv:2609.25333), but two elementary cases in a row do not guarantee a third, and we make no claim beyond $n = 4$.

entry.title: Coherent Information Deletion: Bayesian, Generalized Bayesian and Possibilistic Unlearning

link.title: Coherent Information Deletion: Bayesian, Generalized Bayesian and Possibilistic Unlearning

entry.content:
Bayes’ theorem admits an information processing interpretation due to Zellner (1988): under the Shannon information criterion, the posterior is the unique rule that processes prior and data information without information loss. We revisit these ideas from the perspective of information deletion. Given a posterior based on a complete dataset, what distribution should replace it when a subset of the data is removed? For ordinary Bayesian inference, we show that the corresponding information deletion objective is uniquely minimized by the leave-data-out posterior. We then extend the framework beyond likelihood-based inference from Bayes to the generalized Bayesian updating of Bissiri et al.(2016} based on loss functions. Requiring deletion to be coherent under sequential removal of loss contributions yields a deletion rule that exactly recovers the generalized posterior based only on the retained information. We further develop an axiomatic theory, beyond probabilistic inference, for possibilistic deletion and show that the same information-deletion perspective leads to a principled rule for exact possibilistic unlearning. Finally, restricting these exact deletion principles to tractable families leads naturally to variational Bayesian, generalized Bayesian, and maxitive possibilistic unlearning.

Read more

entry.title: Cointegrated Regressors: Where Folded Concave Penalties Go Beyond LASSO

link.title: Cointegrated Regressors: Where Folded Concave Penalties Go Beyond LASSO

entry.content:
LASSO is one of the most popular regularization methods for high-dimensional regression models. While cointegration is common in practical applications of predictive regressions with many regressors, the convex penalty of LASSO overly suppresses the coefficients of cointegrated regressors and therefore fails to deliver consistent parameter estimation. We employ folded concave penalties (FCP), including the well-known SCAD and MCP, to address this issue. Using FCP, we establish two asymptotic results: (i) a local oracle property for the penalized regression, and (ii) a global oracle property for regressions with a penalty-level constraint. In particular, the latter guarantees a global solution that consistently estimates the true coefficients and enjoys oracle prediction performance. Simulation studies and an application to predicting the euro area unemployment rate show that FCP improves variable selection and out-of-sample prediction relative to LASSO.

Read more

entry.title: Comparing randomized trials

link.title: Comparing randomized trials

entry.content:
Disagreements between randomized trials that address the same causal question pose challenges for the interpretation and synthesis of evidence. We sketch a causal framework for comparing the results of randomized trials that explicitly accommodates the possibility of trial engagement effects. Using counterfactual outcomes defined under joint interventions on treatment assignment and trial-related actions, we compare trial-native treatment effects with the effects transported from one trial to the population of another in a common target population. We show that standard conditions for transporting treatment effects across trial populations are not sufficient to guarantee agreement between transported and trial-native effects. Agreement additionally requires conditions governing how trial-related actions affect outcome across studies - for example, absence of trial engagement effects, equivalence of such effects across trials, or lack of interaction between trial engagement and treatment assignment. Our framework clarifies potential sources of disagreement across trials and extends existing approaches to study comparison to settings in which trial engagement effects may be present.

Read more

entry.title: Complexity Dependent Error Rates for Physics-informed Statistical Learning via the Small-ball Method

link.title: Complexity Dependent Error Rates for Physics-informed Statistical Learning via the Small-ball Method

entry.content:
Physics-informed statistical learning (PISL) integrates empirical data with physical knowledge to enhance the statistical performance of estimators. While PISL methods are widely used in practice, a comprehensive theoretical understanding of how informed regularization affects statistical properties is still missing. Specifically, two fundamental questions have yet to be fully addressed: (A) what is the trade-off between soft penalties and hard constraints, and (B) what is the statistical gain of incorporating physical knowledge compared to purely data-driven empirical error minimisation. In this paper, we address these questions for PISL in classes of functions whose convex hull satisfies a small-ball condition, in particular convex classes, under physical knowledge expressed as linear equations by developing appropriate complexity dependent error rates based on the small-ball method. We specialise them to linear classes of finite dimension $q$ in which the space of solutions of the equation has dimension $k < q$, and show that (A) the physics-informed estimator attains the error bound of the hard-constrained empirical error minimiser whenever the penalty parameter is above an explicit threshold, and that (B) the penalty improves the error rate from $\sqrt{q/n}$ to $\sqrt{k/n}$ under a second moment condition on the noise only, having the effect of a dimensionality reduction. We also quantify how these conclusions degrade when the equation is misspecified, in terms of the excess residual of the target function. This work establishes a theoretical framework for evaluating the statistical properties of physics-informed estimators in such classes, contributing to closing the gap between statistical theory and practical PISL.

Read more

entry.title: Compression Hurts, Pooling Helps: Information Loss in Rayleigh-Scale Estimation from B-Mode Ultrasound

link.title: Compression Hurts, Pooling Helps: Information Loss in Rayleigh-Scale Estimation from B-Mode Ultrasound

entry.content:
Clinical B-mode images are widely available as potential data sources for quantitative ultrasound (QUS) analysis for tissue characterization. However, standard clinical ultrasound devices apply unknown log-compression to RF envelope data before display and storage. Previous work has demonstrated estimation of the underlying RF envelope statistics in the presence of an unknown compression law. Using Fisher information analysis, we show that finite-offset log compression causes severe information loss when estimating the Rayleigh scale $\sigma$, which controls diffuse speckle. For a single image window, unknown compression raises the minimum achievable variance for unbiased estimation of $\sigma$ by a compression-independent factor of approximately 34.98. When $M$ equal-sized windows share the same unknown compression settings, the excess variance decays as $1/M$; even in the most favorable regime, reducing the variance inflation factor below 1.1 requires 340 windows. Our analysis treats the contrast parameter $a$ as unknown and the boundary offset $b$ as known; estimating $b$ experimentally shows even larger variance. We validate this theory using synthetic estimation experiments and demonstrate RF-scale recovery on real RF-envelope windows from the OASBUD dataset. Together, these results clarify the limitations of using routine B-mode images for QUS.

Read more

entry.title: Concentration inequalities for leave-one-out cross validation

link.title: Concentration inequalities for leave-one-out cross validation

entry.content:
In this article we prove that estimator stability, together with a gradient-growth condition on the expected fitted loss, is enough to provide concentration bounds for leave-one-out cross-validation in a general framework. In particular, we provide concentration bounds beyond Lipschitz continuity assumptions on the loss or on the estimator. We obtain our results by relying on random variables with distribution satisfying the logarithmic Sobolev inequality, providing us a relatively rich class of distributions. We illustrate our method by considering several interesting examples, including linear regression, kernel density estimation, and stabilized/truncated estimators such as stabilized kernel regression.

Read more

entry.title: Conditional validity of prediction-powered inference for spatially dependent finite populations

link.title: Conditional validity of prediction-powered inference for spatially dependent finite populations

entry.content:
Prediction-powered inference (PPI) combines full-frame predictions with a small labelled sample to estimate finite-population regression coefficients. We establish conditions for the conditional validity of existing calibrated residual-regression PPI estimators under nonuniform label acquisition and spatially dependent prediction errors. Approximate calibration can leave a population-specific displacement: the projection of prediction errors onto coefficient-specific calibration defects. We characterize its role in conditional inference through the noncentrality of a fixed-candidate Wald region. The relevant target-weight function is the coefficient loading divided by acquisition intensity. When mean-approximation error does not dominate, directional covariance control yields a wider sufficient recovery regime than a total residual-energy bound. A bounded spectral-basis theorem gives conditional coverage under directional covariance, tail and nondegeneracy conditions, with Gaussian and bounded non-Gaussian spatial examples. The analysis accounts for estimation of the one-step augmentation and permits same-label selection from a fixed finite library with a common first-order influence vector. A periodic Fourier construction attains the stochastic directional-gap order within a restricted dictionary class. Constructed and real-record-set experiments illustrate why mean calibration need not protect a slope. The results concern descriptive census projection coefficients under the stated sampling and field conditions.

Read more

entry.title: Conformal Certification of Reasoning Trace Prefixes

link.title: Conformal Certification of Reasoning Trace Prefixes

entry.content:
Language model reasoning traces are rarely all-or-nothing; they frequently contain valid intermediate steps before a critical error occurs. Existing uncertainty quantification methods typically certify final answers or entire responses, failing to provide statistical guarantees for the proportion of a sequential trace that can be safely retained. To address this, we introduce CROP (Conformal Reasoning Output Prefixes), a verifier-agnostic calibration procedure for clean-prefix certification. Given any step-level risk proxy, CROP selects a calibrated threshold and returns the longest contiguous prefix whose step risk proxies remain below it, routing the uncertified suffix for downstream review or repair. Assuming exchangeability, CROP rigorously controls the marginal probability that the returned prefix contains an annotated error. Across six process-labeled reasoning datasets, we demonstrate that standard step-level metrics such as AUROC do not fully capture prefix utility, suggesting verifiers should instead be evaluated by certified prefix length. Furthermore, CROP balances over- and under-withholding and improves downstream repair accuracy by preserving valid intermediate reasoning while discarding misleading suffixes. Ultimately, this work positions prefix certification as a rigorous, practical bridge between process supervision, abstention, and repair. Code available at https://github.com/matthewyccheung/crop.

Read more

entry.title: Consensus-level substitution rates are distinct from the virion-level rate

link.title: Consensus-level substitution rates are distinct from the virion-level rate

entry.content:
Estimating viral substitution rates is central to evolutionary epidemiology, and recent interest in within-host evolution has sharpened the question of what such rates measure. I distinguish two classes of evolutionary rate estimand that are rarely separated in phylogenetic analysis: the virion-level substitution rate (VLSR), a molecular quantity counting mutational events along lineages, and consensus-level substitution rates (CLSRs), population-summary quantities counting allele frequency threshold crossings from below. CLSRs are indexed by the consensus-generation rule. The VLSR and CLSRs are both biologically meaningful, but not interchangeable. Because the consensus-generation rule defines a given CLSR, it should be reported routinely. This reflection should help analysts make more informed methodological choices when working with sets of virus sequences.

Read more

entry.title: Consistent and scalable detection and comparison of spatial patterns

link.title: Consistent and scalable detection and comparison of spatial patterns

entry.content:
Spatial omics maps molecular features within tissues to study their organization across biological contexts, including disease and development. Interpreting these maps requires distinguishing patterns from noise and comparing them across samples. Yet pattern detection remains unresolved, and comparisons based on regional summaries lose spatial detail. Here we show that spatial frequency provides a common basis for detecting and comparing these patterns. Our framework, SONIC, unifies spatial detection tests through a common quadratic form, establishes conditions for reliable detection and explains how kernel choice determines sensitivity to different spatial patterns. It also separates changes in spatial organization from changes in overall abundance without aligning tissues. Fast, memory-efficient algorithms make detection and comparison practical across large datasets. Applying SONIC, we identify plaque-associated responses in Alzheimer’s disease and differences in the spatial expression of blood-clotting genes between glioma subtypes. We further construct a gene-centric atlas that traces changes in spatial expression through mouse and human embryogenesis and supports retrieval of related patterns across species. These results extend spatial analysis from identifying individual patterns to following their changes across anatomically different tissues. Together, SONIC establishes a shared language for integrating molecular maps across studies and technologies.

Read more

entry.title: Continuous-Speech Parkinson’s Disease Detection Using Acoustic and Inharmonicity Features

link.title: Continuous-Speech Parkinson’s Disease Detection Using Acoustic and Inharmonicity Features

entry.content:
Notable efforts have been made to identify Parkinson’s disease (PD) from vocal data, primarily using sustained vowel phonations. In this work, we extend on these efforts introducing a PD identification approach for continuous speech, enabling a practical background monitoring of voice data to detect vocal changes indicative of PD. Using two distinct data sets, we compare the best sustained vowel model with that of the proposed continuous speech model, clearly illustrating the preferential performance of the latter. We examine approaches for speaker level evaluation and data leakage preventions, as well as how vowel information may be reliably extracted from continuous speech. The proposed method framework exploits both traditional acoustic representations and a promising novel inharmonicity based framework, showing how the latter provides complementary information improving the performance for one of the data sets; however, for the other data set, this information did not significantly improve (nor reduce) the performance, suggesting that further studies are required before being able to draw firm conclusions in its use. Overall, the work clearly illustrates the benefit of forming PD classification using continuous speech compared to using sustained vowel sounds.

Read more

entry.title: Control Consistency Losses for Diffusion Bridges

link.title: Control Consistency Losses for Diffusion Bridges

entry.content:
Simulating the conditioned dynamics of diffusion processes, given their initial and terminal states, is an important but challenging problem in the sciences. The difficulty is particularly pronounced for rare events, for which the unconditioned dynamics rarely reach the terminal state. In this work, we propose a novel approach for learning diffusion bridges based on a self-consistency property of the optimal control. The resulting algorithm learns the conditioned dynamics in an iterative online manner, and exhibits strong performance in a range of empirical settings without requiring differentiation through simulated trajectories. Beyond the diffusion bridge setting, we draw connections between our self-consistency framework and recent advances in the wider stochastic optimal control literature.

Read more

entry.title: Convergence-Rate-Guided Algorithm Design of Expected Improvement for Continuous Simulation Optimization

link.title: Convergence-Rate-Guided Algorithm Design of Expected Improvement for Continuous Simulation Optimization

entry.content:
Expected improvement (EI) based on stochastic kriging (SK) surrogate is widely used in continuous simulation optimization, but unknown heteroscedastic noise on simulation output makes three basic design choices consequential: the incumbent used to define improvement, the replication level at each sampled point, and the terminal recommendation. Existing methods typically either assume the noise levels are known or choose these components separately through heuristic rules or empirical calibration. We instead derive a high-probability upper bound on the simple regret and systematically choose the three components within general rule classes to tighten this bound. We first establish a finite-sample confidence bound for the SK predictor with unknown and estimated noise levels as a foundation for the three design choices. We then analyze general posterior-quantile families for both the incumbent and the terminal recommendation. For the incumbent, minimizing the regret bound selects a lower quantile coefficient that matches the coefficient in the SK predictor confidence bound. For the terminal recommendation, minimizing the same bound instead selects the sampled point with the best upper posterior quantile under the same coefficient. These opposite quantile choices reflect the different roles of search and implementation in simulation optimization. Intermediate simulations are exploratory with an optimistic incumbent, while the terminal recommendation is implemented in the real system and is therefore relatively conservative about the remaining posterior uncertainty. Under mild conditions satisfied by common kernels, minimizing a tractable kernel-specific bound yields $\Theta(\log T)$ replications. To our knowledge, this is the first simple-regret guarantee for a continuous-domain EI-type simulation optimization method that learns unknown heteroscedastic variances through replications.

Read more

entry.title: Copula Active Subspaces II: Error Decomposition, A Posteriori Estimation, and Sharpness of the Bounds

link.title: Copula Active Subspaces II: Error Decomposition, A Posteriori Estimation, and Sharpness of the Bounds

entry.content:
The Copula Active Subspaces (CAS) method of Part I estimates a non-Gaussian observation-noise density $\pi_{\boldsymbol{n}}$ from residual samples. Its KL divergence $\mathcal{D}{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi{\boldsymbol{n}}\,|\,\widehat\pi_{\boldsymbol{n}})$ admits an exact decomposition into marginal, projection and reduced-density terms and bounds the posterior KL divergence averaged over the true predictive distribution. We derive a priori bounds for these terms, together with estimates or bounds from residual samples. Weighted nearest-neighbour entropy estimates are used for the marginal and reduced-density terms, with asymptotic standard errors in exact rank coordinates. For the projection error, the score is fitted on one subsample, and its mean squared magnitude outside the retained subspace is estimated on the other. Corrections for score and rank-transform errors then give a theoretical upper bound with probability at least $1-\delta$. Tests on three known noise laws in dimension $d=20$ use the estimated rank transform. In $11$ of $12$ combinations of example and sample size, the sum of the two estimated terms and the trace bound exceeds the reference divergence after averaging over the estimated models. In these tests, score-estimation error is the largest contribution to looseness. The overestimate from the Gaussian log-Sobolev inequality alone is at most a factor of $1.98$.

Read more

entry.title: Counterfactual Certification for Sequential Unlearning with Long-Run Performance Guarantees

link.title: Counterfactual Certification for Sequential Unlearning with Long-Run Performance Guarantees

entry.content:
Certified machine unlearning ensures the proximity between the unlearned model and a model retrained without the data to be forgotten. Extending this framework to sequential deletion requests, typically arriving as groups of variable size (e.g., all records of one user or of coordinated users), is challenging. For unlearning methods based on fine-tuning on the retain sets, this leads to either degrading performance or increasing computation as the number of unlearning requests grows. For independent successive requests, we instead certify each model release against a counterfactual unlearning trajectory in which the group being deleted never took part. With a fixed fine-tuning budget per deletion, we show that, for smooth strongly convex objectives, this approach keeps the performance loss bounded, uniformly in the number of requests. Experiments with multiclass logistic regression on FEMNIST show that the resulting algorithm needs fewer corrective steps than existing sequential methods and outperforms training-time differential privacy, particularly when group sizes are heterogeneous.

Read more

entry.title: Cover meets Robbins while Betting on Bounded Data: $\ln n$ Regret and Almost Sure $\ln\ln n$ Regret

link.title: Cover meets Robbins while Betting on Bounded Data: $\ln n$ Regret and Almost Sure $\ln\ln n$ Regret

entry.content:
Consider betting against a sequence of $[0,1]$-valued observations using bets that are fair if the data have a conditional mean $m_0 \in (0,1)$. Cover’s universal portfolio algorithm achieves a worst-case regret of $O(\ln n)$ compared to the best constant bet in hindsight, and this logarithmic order is unimprovable against adversarial data. We construct an explicit full-support Robbins mixture that combines insights from Robbins and Cover. It retains $O(\ln n)$ regret on every path while also eventually satisfying $R_n\le(1+o(1))\ln\ln V_n$ on every path with bounded mixture wealth and $V_n\to\infty$, where $V_n$ is an intrinsic variance process. It also attains the optimal asymptotic wealth growth rate under iid alternatives. Under the conditional-mean claim and almost-sure divergence of $V_n$, the sharper regret bound holds almost surely, and its leading constant $1$ is unimprovable. We also give explicit finite-time, path-wise regret bounds. A simple hedging principle shows how splitting initial wealth between two strategies achieves a best-of-both-worlds guarantee by retaining the smaller of their regrets and the larger of their growth rates. We contrast our results to those for unbounded data in Agrawal and Ramdas (2026). Their worst-case regret is unbounded. However, hedging yields almost-sure iterated-logarithmic regret together with optimal growth. Finally, our wealth process witnesses a sharp game-theoretic upper law of iterated logarithm, analogous to Shafer and Vovk (2005).

Read more

entry.title: DCD: Decomposition-based Causal Discovery from Autocorrelated and Non-Stationary Temporal Data

link.title: DCD: Decomposition-based Causal Discovery from Autocorrelated and Non-Stationary Temporal Data

entry.content:
Multivariate time series in domains such as finance, climate science, and healthcare often exhibit long-term trends, seasonal patterns, and short-term fluctuations, complicating causal inference under non-stationarity and autocorrelation. Existing causal discovery methods typically operate on raw observations, making them vulnerable to spurious edges and misattributed temporal dependencies. We introduce a decomposition-based causal discovery framework that separates each time series into trend, seasonal, and residual components and performs component-specific causal analysis. Trend components are assessed using stationarity tests, seasonal components using kernel-based dependence measures, and residual components using constraint-based causal discovery. The resulting component-level graphs are integrated into a unified multi-scale causal structure. This approach isolates long- and short-range causal effects, reduces spurious associations, and improves interpretability. Across extensive synthetic benchmarks and real-world climate data, our framework more accurately recovers ground-truth causal structure than state-of-the-art baselines, particularly under strong non-stationarity and temporal autocorrelation.

Read more

entry.title: Dangers of Bayesian analyses and how to address them

link.title: Dangers of Bayesian analyses and how to address them

entry.content:
In light of the US FDA announcement supporting the use of Bayesian methods in clinical trials, we present a nontechnical review of problems with Bayesian analyses and methods to address them. Our focus is on the well-known sensitivities of Bayesian results to biases embedded in their prior distributions. This vulnerability calls for special safety features, including detailed justification of informative priors based on empirical-research literature rather than on singular expert opinions. Crucially, the information contributed by priors should be realistic in light of actual background data rather than merely judged so by available experts. We illustrate our recommendations with using a textbook clinical-trial example which covered these points. We then use the example describe basic diagnostic procedures and safety recommendations for Bayesian analyses and their presentation. These include reference analyses which exclude informative priors, and justification for informative priors based on empirical-research literature rather than on philosophical arguments. We also critique some common priors that violate our realism requirements. One strategy to aid judgments about priors is to translate them into data to be added to the study data. The source of these prior data should be examined with the same critical attitude as the source of study data. We illustrate some simple summary methods for comparing prior and data information, including prior predictions of data, variance ratios, and their translation to effective sample sizes (ESS). Finally, we argue that Bayesian analyses should be treated as extensions or supplements to conventional analyses, rather than replace them, for that treatment puts prior construction and justification at the fore of the transition from frequentist to Bayesian analyses in teaching and practice.

Read more

entry.title: Data-Topology Compatibility Enables Personalization in Decentralized Learning

link.title: Data-Topology Compatibility Enables Personalization in Decentralized Learning

entry.content:
Decentralized learning must balance collaboration with personalization across heterogeneous agents. This paper studies when cooperation can support statistically coherent groups of personalized models. We show that data-topology compatibility enables robust orbit-wise personalization: when local objectives and communication topology have (approximately) compatible automorphisms, agents within an orbit share (approximately) equal limiting distributions, while different orbits remain distinct without explicit personalization. This creates a new intermediate regime between global consensus and independent local learning. Under exact data-topology compatibility, as a reference system, we decompose the stochastic learning dynamics into orbit-level and transverse components, derive a necessary and sufficient stability criterion for distributional synchronization, and characterize the orbit-structured stationary law. Modelling an approximate data-topology compatible system as an $\varepsilon$-perturbed reference system, we prove the introduced errors have uniform-in-time and stationary $O(\varepsilon)$ bounds in 2-Wasserstein distance. We also prove sufficient conditions for lower stationary average excess risk than both independent local training and the best single shared parameter. Experiments on synthetic data, MNIST, and CIFAR-10 are in full agreement with the theory. The code is available at https://github.com/Veronicaaa1/orbit-personalization.

Read more

entry.title: De-biased Distribution Estimation for Locally Differential Private Survival Data

link.title: De-biased Distribution Estimation for Locally Differential Private Survival Data

entry.content:
Sharing time-to-event data can leak sensitive information about individual participants in clinical studies. To protect the privacy of data, differential privacy (DP) framework offers rigorous protection for data sharing. The local variant of differential privacy is particularly appealing because each record is perturbed before it leaves the data owner or contributor. However, the injected perturbation distorts the true distribution of the source data, yielding low utility and invalid statistical inference with the released data. In this work, we propose a nonparametric estimator for the true survivor function via the deconvolution kernel function with locally differential private (LDP) right-censored survival data in which both the event times and the event indicators are privatized. Our estimator simultaneously de-biases the perturbation applied to the times and the errors induced by flipping the event indicators due to LDP. Theoretically, we establish the uniform consistency and point-wise asymptotic normality of the de-biased distribution estimator, and derive its uniform convergence rate together with the optimal bandwidth attaining that rate. Simulation studies and the analysis of a semi-synthetic dataset generated from the METABRIC breast cancer cohort demonstrate the performance of the proposed estimator across privacy budgets, censoring levels, and sample sizes. By the post-processing property of DP, the proposed de-biased estimator inherits the privacy guarantee while restoring valid inference on the survivor function.

Read more

entry.title: Decomposing A Neural Learner

link.title: Decomposing A Neural Learner

entry.content:
Neural learners for classification and regression are often criticized as black boxes. We propose a probabilistic decomposition of neural learners that accounts for heterogeneous predictability across the feature space. A training procedure combining the EM algorithm, stochastic gradient descent, and maximum likelihood estimation is developed to jointly learn the predictable component and an input-dependent reliability score. We show that the optimal decomposed learner recovers the response distribution within the predictable component, while the reliability score characterizes the predictability of individual observations. We further extend the framework to incorporate localized feature transformations. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

Read more

entry.title: Decomposing Basketball Team Efficiency Using the Four Factors and Shapley Values

link.title: Decomposing Basketball Team Efficiency Using the Four Factors and Shapley Values

entry.content:
Understanding how different aspects of basketball performance translate into overall team efficiency is central to analysis and strategy. This paper derives a mathematical expression that presents team offensive, defensive, and net ratings directly in terms of a team’s four factors and shooting percentages. The resulting formula captures the full nonlinear structure of how shooting, turnovers, rebounding, and free throws jointly interact to determine team efficiency. Using this relationship, we introduce a Shapley value-based framework that decomposes team net rating into a sum of contributions from individual factors. This way, different facets of the game are made commensurable. The decomposition requires only standard box-score statistics and a single parameter $\mu$, which represents the relative frequency of possession-ending free throws and remains constant for a given league and season. Consequently, it can be applied equally to individual games, full seasons, or league-wide trends. Moreover, it is immediately applicable to box-score statistics from any league or competition level by a simple change of reference point and the estimation of league- and season-specific parameter $\mu$. Empirical analyses using NBA data from 2000 to 2025 validate the offensive ratings produced by the formula against exact play-by-play data, showing a nearly perfect correlation ($r = 0.999$) and a low Mean Absolute Error of $0.188$ points per 100 possessions. These analyses further illustrate how the proposed framework can be used to quantify how teams achieve success in different ways or to explain the results of individual games.

Read more

entry.title: Decomposing the spectral density function of an ARMA process

link.title: Decomposing the spectral density function of an ARMA process

entry.content:
Quasi-periodic oscillations are characterized by fitting Lorentzian functions to a nonparametric estimate of the power spectral density, a two-step procedure that separates estimation from modeling and does not accommodate measurement error. We develop a parametric alternative based on autoregressive moving-average (ARMA) processes observed with measurement error. We derive an exact decomposition of the ARMA spectral density into real-valued components, one for each class of autoregressive roots under complex conjugation, plus a polynomial term when the moving-average order is at least the autoregressive order. Each component is a Wrapped Cauchy kernel, and for complex roots it is accompanied by a conjugate-Poisson term that makes the peak asymmetric and displaces its maximum from the frequency given by the argument of the root. We obtain closed-form expressions for the location, height, width, and asymmetry of each peak, and a matching variance decomposition. Parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood through the Kalman filter, and all descriptors follow by plug-in. Simulations show that the closed-form peak location is recovered without appreciable bias. An X-ray binary light curve illustrates the methodology.

Read more

entry.title: Deep Jump Gaussian Processes for Surrogate Modeling of High-Dimensional Piecewise Continuous Functions

link.title: Deep Jump Gaussian Processes for Surrogate Modeling of High-Dimensional Piecewise Continuous Functions

entry.content:
We introduce Deep Jump Gaussian Processes (DJGP), a novel method for surrogate modeling of a piecewise continuous function on a high-dimensional domain. DJGP addresses the limitations of conventional Jump Gaussian Processes (JGP) in high-dimensional input spaces by integrating region-specific, locally linear projections with JGP modeling. These projections employ region-dependent matrices to capture local low-dimensional subspace structures, making them well suited to the inherently localized modeling behavior of JGPs, a variant of local Gaussian processes. To control model complexity, we place a Gaussian Process prior on the projection matrices, allowing them to evolve smoothly across the input space. The projected inputs are then modeled with a JGP to capture piecewise continuous relationships with the response. This yields a distinctive two-layer deep learning of GP/JGP. We further develop a scalable variational inference algorithm to jointly learn the projection matrices and JGP hyperparameters. Rigorous theoretical analysis and extensive empirical studies are provided to justify the proposed approach. In particular, we derive an oracle error bound for DJGP and decompose it into four distinct sources of error, which are then linked to practical implications. Experiments on synthetic and benchmark datasets demonstrate that DJGP achieves superior predictive accuracy and more reliable uncertainty quantification compared with existing methods.

Read more

entry.title: Deep Neural Mixed Models for Nonlinear Longitudinal Prediction with Subject-Specific Heterogeneity

link.title: Deep Neural Mixed Models for Nonlinear Longitudinal Prediction with Subject-Specific Heterogeneity

entry.content:
Longitudinal health data often exhibit within-subject correlation, subject-specific heterogeneity, and complex nonlinear predictor–response relationships that may not be adequately captured by conventional mixed models. We propose a Deep Generalized Neural Network Mixed Model (DGNMM) that extends the GLMM framework by using a deep neural network to learn nonlinear population-level relationships while incorporating directly trainable, regularized subject-specific effects to capture individual heterogeneity. The model is estimated using prediction-oriented stochastic optimization with separate regularization of the neural-network parameters and subject-specific effects. This formulation allows us to investigate when increased nonlinear representation capacity provides additional predictive benefit in the presence of subject-specific heterogeneity. A simulation study varies population-level nonlinearity and subject-specific heterogeneity and compares DGNMM with GLMM, artificial neural network (ANN), Maity–Pal (MP), and GNMM alternatives for continuous and binary longitudinal outcomes. In the real-data application, DGNMM achieved the lowest MSPE for continuous depression and anxiety prediction, while alternative models remained competitive for binary outcomes. Exploratory subject-level analyses showed heterogeneous predictive gains across individuals, but the magnitude of the estimated subject-specific effects was not significantly associated with predictive gain. Overall, increased nonlinear representation capacity was most beneficial for continuous prediction under nonlinear response structures, while greater subject-specific heterogeneity did not systematically yield larger predictive gains.

Read more

entry.title: Deeply unrolled alternating projections for phase retrieval

link.title: Deeply unrolled alternating projections for phase retrieval

entry.content:
Deep unrolling methods for inverse problems augment traditional reconstruction algorithms with learned priors to improve their performance. These methods have been developed under the implicit assumption that the geometry of the measurement operator does not change between training and deployment; when this is no longer the case, the quality of obtained reconstructions can degrade significantly. In this paper, we argue that this is not an inherent limitation of the deep unrolling paradigm and can be mitigated by a careful choice of the underlying iterative algorithm. We propose a deep unrolling framework for the phase retrieval problem that augments the alternating projections method with a learned denoising step. Our method obtains high-quality reconstructions without the need for retraining in settings where conventional model-based alternatives struggle, such as when the dynamic range of the measurement operator changes significantly at test time.

Read more

entry.title: Density Ratio Estimation with Stein Displacement Fields

link.title: Density Ratio Estimation with Stein Displacement Fields

entry.content:
Density ratios quantify distribution shift from a probability-mass point of view, whereas displacement fields describe, from a dynamical point of view, how one distribution is transported onto another. Although both offer complementary insights, they are usually estimated separately, and converting one into the other requires post-processing. In this paper, we estimate the density ratio between a target and a base distribution by parametrizing it through a displacement field acting on the base: the log-ratio is modeled as minus the Stein operator of the base applied to the field, up to a normalizing constant. This gives both statistical and dynamical descriptions of the distribution shift through a single convex optimization problem. Iterating this estimate-and-move step gives two inference algorithms: push-forward moves the model and corrects a pretrained sampler without retraining it, whereas pull-back moves the data closer to the base and fits a transformation model one layer at a time. Applications to distribution shift in simulation-based inference and to nonlinear independent component analysis illustrate the benefits and limitations of the approach.

Read more

entry.title: Dependent Dirichlet processes via thinning

link.title: Dependent Dirichlet processes via thinning

entry.content:
When analyzing data from multiple sources, it is often convenient to strike a careful balance between two goals: capturing the heterogeneity of the samples and sharing information across them. We introduce a novel framework to model a collection of samples using dependent Dirichlet processes constructed through a thinning mechanism. The proposed approach modifies the stick-breaking representation of the Dirichlet process by thinning, that is, setting equal to zero a random subset of the beta random variables used in the original construction. This results in a collection of dependent random distributions that exhibit both shared and unique atoms, with the shared ones assigned distinct weights in each distribution. The generality of the construction allows expressing a wide variety of dependence structures among the elements of the generated random vectors. Moreover, its simplicity facilitates the characterization of several theoretical properties and the derivation of efficient computational methods for posterior inference. A simulation study illustrates how a modeling approach based on the proposed process reduces uncertainty in group-specific inferences while preventing excessive borrowing of information when the data indicate it is unnecessary. This added flexibility improves the accuracy of posterior inference, outperforming related state-of-the-art models. An application to the Collaborative Perinatal Project data highlights the model’s capability to estimate group-specific densities and uncover a meaningful partition of the observations, both within and across samples, providing valuable insights into the underlying data structure.

Read more

entry.title: Design-based theory for covariate adjustment in generalized pairwise comparisons

link.title: Design-based theory for covariate adjustment in generalized pairwise comparisons

entry.content:
Generalized pairwise comparisons summarize treatment effects in randomized experiments with ordinal, multivariate, or prioritized outcomes. We study optimal covariate adjustment under complete randomization, with potential outcomes and covariates fixed and treatment assignment as the sole source of randomness. We derive the exact randomization variance of the unadjusted estimator and characterize linear calibration adjustments using the between-arm difference in covariate means. The asymptotic variance is a strictly convex quadratic in the adjustment coefficient, yielding a closed-form optimum. The resulting estimator is asymptotically no less efficient than the unadjusted estimator, with an explicit precision gain that clarifies which covariates improve precision. However, natural pair-level and single-arm least squares adjustments generally use weights that differ from the allocation-dependent optimum and can substantially reduce efficiency. We also propose a within-arm variance estimator for asymptotically conservative inference, whose conservatism arises from unidentifiable joint variation in a unit’s two potential scores, and show that residualizing each arm on its own projection coefficient saves the discrepancy that governs the efficiency loss of conventional adjustments. In the special case where the comparison function is the outcome difference, our proposed covariate-adjusted estimator is first-order equivalent to the fully interacted regression adjustment of Lin (Ann. Appl. Stat., 2013, 7, 295-318).

Read more

entry.title: Designing for Prediction: Planning Formulas for Expected Out-of-Sample $R^2$ and $r$

link.title: Designing for Prediction: Planning Formulas for Expected Out-of-Sample $R^2$ and $r$

entry.content:
Design calculations let researchers gauge, before data is collected, whether a planned study is likely to detect an effect. In this paper, we develop such calculations for predictive models using ordinary least squares and ridge regression under leave-one-out cross-validation. To do so, we derive closed-form expressions relating the expected out-of-sample $R^2$ and the expected correlation between observed and predicted outcomes to four design-stage quantities: sample size, number of predictors, an assumed population $R^2$ ($\rho^2_{in}$) and a design efficiency factor $D^*$ (which summarizes how leverage is distributed across observations). Unlike the classical shrinkage formulas, which depend only on sample size and dimension, these are sensitive to how covariates are arranged – to imbalance and skew. A simulation study assesses the accuracy of the formulas against realized values under a variety of data generating mechanisms. We apply the methods to a published study predicting personality from smartphone behavior and show that the design formulas would have indicated, before any analyses were run, that least squares could not be expected to beat the sample mean while ridge could. An R package, predpower, implements the calculations.

Read more

A simulation study assesses the accuracy of the formulas against realized values under a variety of data generating mechanisms. We apply the methods to a published study predicting personality from smartphone behavior and show that the design formulas would have indicated, before any analyses were run, that least squares could not be expected to beat the sample mean while ridge could. An R package, predpower, implements the calculations.

entry.title: Detecting Impact of the Great Recession on Macroeconomic Indicators

link.title: Detecting Impact of the Great Recession on Macroeconomic Indicators

entry.content:
We study structural changes in multivariate time series by estimating and comparing stationary graphs of macroeconomic time series before and after an economic crisis, such as the Great Recession. Building on a latent time series framework called Orthogonally-rotated Univariate Time-series (OUT), we propose a shared-parameter framework-the spOUT autoregressive model (spOUTAR)-that jointly models two related multivariate time series and enables coherent Bayesian estimation of their corresponding stationary precision matrices. This framework provides a principled mechanism for detecting and quantifying which conditional relationships among the variables changed or formed following the crisis. Specifically, we study the impact of the Great Recession (December 2007-June 2009) that substantially disrupted global and national economies, prompting long-lasting shifts in macroeconomic indicators and their interrelationships. While many studies document its economic consequences, less is known about how the underlying conditional dependency structure among economic variables changed as economies moved from pre-crisis stability through the shock and back to normalcy. Using the proposed approach to analyze U.S. and OECD macroeconomic data, we demonstrate that spOUTAR effectively captures recession-induced changes in stationary graphical structure, offering a flexible and interpretable tool for studying structural shifts in economic systems.

Read more

entry.title: Differentiable Systematic Resampling for Variational Sequential Monte Carlo

link.title: Differentiable Systematic Resampling for Variational Sequential Monte Carlo

entry.content:
Particle filters are a standard tool for nonlinear state estimation, but their resampling step is discrete, preventing gradient-based learning in variational sequential Monte Carlo. We introduce Differentiable Systematic Resampling (DSR), a temperature-controlled relaxation of systematic resampling, that preserves the CDF-ordered, banded structure of systematic resampling while enabling full gradient flow. DSR converges to exact systematic resampling as the temperature vanishes, and we prove a pointwise exponential convergence rate for the induced bias. Compared to optimal-transport-based differentiable resampling, DSR avoids iterative solvers and has substantially lower computational overhead. Experiments on stochastic dynamical systems and real-world handwriting data show that DSR achieves comparable or superior filtering and dynamics learning performance.

Read more

entry.title: Differentially Private Synthetic Data via APIs 3: Using Simulators Instead of Foundation Model

link.title: Differentially Private Synthetic Data via APIs 3: Using Simulators Instead of Foundation Model

entry.content:
Differentially private (DP) synthetic data enables the use of sensitive datasets while providing strong privacy guarantees. Recently, Private Evolution (PE) has emerged as a promising framework for generating DP synthetic data using only inference APIs of foundation models. However, suitable foundation models are not always available for every private data domain. In this paper, we show that PE is more general than previously understood and can incorporate APIs beyond foundation models. In particular, we show that state-of-the-art non-neural-network data synthesizers, including computer graphics-based image generators and physics simulation tools (which we refer to as simulators), integrate naturally into PE. We call the resulting method Sim-PE. Sim-PE broadens the applicability of PE while improving performance. For image synthesis, Sim-PE improves downstream classification accuracy by up to 3x, reduces FID by up to 80%, and is significantly more efficient. We further show that simulators and foundation models can be seamlessly combined within Sim-PE for additional gains. Beyond performance improvements, Sim-PE enables new DP applications that are difficult or impossible for existing methods, including generating DP control signals whose execution reproduces the distribution of private observations. The code is open-sourced in the Private Evolution Python library: https://github.com/microsoft/DPSDA

Read more

entry.title: Direction Preferring Confidence Intervals

link.title: Direction Preferring Confidence Intervals

entry.content:
Confidence intervals (CIs) are fundamental in statistical analysis, providing interval estimates for unknown parameters. We introduce direction-preferring CIs that prioritize inference for parameters with a specific sign (e.g., positive sign). Unlike previous methods of constructing CIs, our intervals are based on the inversion of acceptance regions that differ for positive and negative parameters, to enhance the probability of determining the sign in the prespecified preferred direction while maintaining standard coverage. We apply our suggestion in the typical context that multiple parameters are considered, but only some of the constructed CIs are of interest, e.g., when CIs are reported only for the subset of parameters that are found to differ significantly from zero. This leads us to suggest direction-preferring CIs with false coverage rate (FCR) control, as well as conditional direction-preferring CIs that adjust for selection by conditioning on the selection event. We compare the two selection adjustment methods in theory and using numerical experiments. The procedures we develop are useful for inference on secondary outcomes in medical applications, a setting we highlight through two motivating examples.

Read more

entry.title: Discrete-Time Survival Modelling with Dynamic Industrial Graphs for Mortgage Credit Risk

link.title: Discrete-Time Survival Modelling with Dynamic Industrial Graphs for Mortgage Credit Risk

entry.content:
Mortgage credit risk may exhibit dependence across economically connected areas, even when they are geographically distant. However, current models typically represent cross-area dependence through fixed geographical neighbourhoods, potentially overlooking economic connections that extend beyond physical proximity and evolve over time. These models may fail to capture shared risks among geographically distant but economically similar areas, and cannot describe a changing dependence of risk; it therefore risks retaining economically obsolete connections while omitting newly emerging ones. This paper uses similarities of industrial composition as a measure of economic proximity and develops a discrete-time survival model with dynamic industrial graphs to capture evolving cross-area dependence in mortgage default risk. The resulting graphs are reconstructed annually, allowing both their topology and edge weights to change as regional industrial compositions evolve. Jointly combining a proper conditional autoregressive process with a first-order autoregressive process governs the temporal cross-area dependence and the temporal persistence in latent risk simultaneously. The model is estimated using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation and evaluated on U.S. mortgage loan-level data against the static industrial graph specifications. The results show that the proposed dynamic model achieves better in-sample fit and out-of-sample discrimination, while its estimated parameters indicate substantial graph-induced cross-area dependence and temporal persistence. These findings demonstrate the value of allowing economically defined neighbourhoods to evolve when modelling mortgage default risk.

Read more

entry.title: Distributional Regression for Arbitrary Response Variables Using ReLU Neural Networks

link.title: Distributional Regression for Arbitrary Response Variables Using ReLU Neural Networks

entry.content:
This paper develops a unified framework for distributional regression with arbitrary response variables. Rather than relying on scalar thresholds or Euclidean structure, we model conditional event probabilities indexed by measurable sets, which extends distributional regression to general response spaces while retaining a direct connection to classical event-based formulations. Within this framework, we study two complementary estimators: a preliminary estimator based on separate regression of event indicators, and a constrained estimator that enforces inclusion-consistent predictions through a directed acyclic graph (DAG) over a finite set family. We establish general error bounds for both estimators and further specialize the results to dense ReLU networks, yielding explicit convergence rates overcoming the curse of dimensionality. Simulation studies and real-data experiments further demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the proposed framework.

Read more

entry.title: Dynamic Extended Generalized Many-Facet Rasch Model: A Unified Approach to Rater-Mediated Assessment

link.title: Dynamic Extended Generalized Many-Facet Rasch Model: A Unified Approach to Rater-Mediated Assessment

entry.content:
Rating procedures are crucial in psychological and medical diagnosis, educational assessment, peer review, and grant evaluation. A major methodological challenge is disentangling multiple sources of variability in ratings, such as subject ability, rater behavior, and item characteristics. Item Response Theory-based models, most notably many-facet Rasch models and hierarchical rater models, have been widely adopted for jointly estimating subject, rater, and item effects, while retaining high interpretability. We introduce the Dynamic Extended Generalized Many-Facet Rasch model, a general class of Bayesian semiparametric models that integrate and extend existing approaches. Its measurement model allows location and discrimination parameters to depend jointly on item and rater characteristics and incorporates subject-item and rater-subject variation. The dynamic extension introduces a rater-specific cross-lagged effect capturing dependence on the previously rated subject, and a Bayesian P-spline capturing systematic changes in discrimination over the rating sequence, accounting for learning, fatigue, or adaptation effects. Subject heterogeneity is addressed through Bayesian nonparametric mixtures, flexibly learning the latent ability distribution without strict parametric assumptions and enabling model-based subject clustering. We also derive a closed-form, model-based inter-rater consensus coefficient and study its characteristics. We discuss theoretical properties, develop posterior computation strategies, and evaluate the model in simulation studies and two real-data applications.

Read more

entry.title: E-Backtesting Expected Shortfall without Value-at-Risk Forecasts under Time-series Models

link.title: E-Backtesting Expected Shortfall without Value-at-Risk Forecasts under Time-series Models

entry.content:
Expected Shortfall (ES) measures the average size of tail losses. Its sequential backtests typically also require a Value-at-Risk (VaR) forecast. We develop two e-backtesting methods using only observed losses and ES forecasts: one for iid losses only and the other for time series under an AR-GARCH conditional VaR structure. Under the stated assumptions, both control false rejections at any stopping time. For the time-series method, validity requires a fixed parameter–quantile pair representing the conditional VaR path and a positive report margin. The time-series statistic takes an infimum over possible parameter and VaR values. We choose the betting process $(\lambda_t)$ by maximizing an empirical growth rate averaged across candidate parameters. We compute the statistic by continuous VaR profiling on a dense parameter grid. For grid approximations, we prove convergence to the continuous infimum, together with convergence of the probability of false rejection, as the grid is refined over a fixed monitoring period. Lower and upper bounds for the VaR infimum on the parameter grid control the accuracy of the numerical profiling. Simulations, including ES reports that change from over-reporting to under-reporting, and an application to daily NASDAQ losses provide numerical comparisons with VaR–ES e-processes and fixed-sample ES backtests, assessing detection frequencies and the timing of rejections.

Read more

entry.title: Effect of Spherical Parameter Space on Number of Non-Forgetting Tasks and Capacity of Continual Learning

link.title: Effect of Spherical Parameter Space on Number of Non-Forgetting Tasks and Capacity of Continual Learning

entry.content:
We propose a continuous learning formulation for $T$ non-forgetting tasks with the spherical parameter space $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}(\sqrt{d})$ in asymptotic regime $d\rightarrow \infty$. Each task $i$ has an optimum $\bm{\Theta}i$, minimizing its corresponding loss function $R_i(\bm{w})$ on sphere. We reduce each task $i$ to an acceptable loss region modeled by a geodesic ball $B{\bm{\Theta}i}(r_i(d))$ on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}(\sqrt{d})$ centered at $\bm{\Theta}_i$ with radius $r_i(d)$. To model task dependencies (similarities), task optima $\bm{\Theta}_i$ are distributed by a Neyman-Scott clustered point process $\Phi$. Cluster centers ${\bm{Y}_j}{j=1}^{N_p}$ form a homogeneous Poisson point process on sphere, while intra-cluster task optima follow a von Mises-Fisher distribution with mean $\bm{Y}j$ and concentration $\kappa$. Each task $t\in {1, …, T}$ learning algorithm is considered to be a channel $Q{t}(\mathrm{d}\bm{w}_t \bm{w}{t-1}, \mathcal{K}{t-1}(\bm{\theta}{1:t-1}), \bm{\theta}_t)$, where $\bm{W}_t$ is the learned parameter of task $t$ and $\mathcal{K}{t-1}(\bm{\Theta}{1:t-1})=\bigcap{i=1}^{t-1}B_{\bm{\Theta}i}(r_i(d))$. Since in continual learning, the learner does not need to reach $\bm{\Theta}_t$ exactly to successfully learn task $t$, to avoid forgetting as well as reliable learning, it only needs for the learned parameter vector $\bm{W}{t}$ to enter $B_{\bm{\Theta}t}(r_t(d)) \cap \mathcal{K}{t-1}(\bm{\Theta}{1:t-1})$. Using this model, we derive an upper bound on $T$ ensuring $\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{K}{T}(\bm{\Theta}_{1:T}) \neq \emptyset] \rightarrow 1$ as $d\rightarrow \infty$ and $\kappa/d \rightarrow \alpha$, where $\alpha>0$ is a constant. Finally, for $T$ tasks sampled uniformly from $\Phi$, we derive an upper bound for total information theoretic capacity under the non-forgetting constraint for each task.

Read more

entry.title: Energy-Guided Learning for Heat Equation with Noisy Source: Optimal Estimation and Generalization Bounds

link.title: Energy-Guided Learning for Heat Equation with Noisy Source: Optimal Estimation and Generalization Bounds

entry.content:
Data and the governing partial differential equations (PDEs) of continuous-time dynamical systems provide rich structure for statistical learning. A central challenge is how to integrate data with PDE constraints in a principled way to improve generalization. In this paper, we characterize the statistical estimation and generalization properties of learning solutions to the heat equation with a noisy source function from finite, randomly sampled data. We first derive a novel variational formulation, which we characterize as the minimizer of loss function for an energy regularized and ellipticity debiased Sobolev regression. By formulating the learning task as a supervised problem over space-time domains under physically meaningful norms, our approach goes beyond the traditional supervised learning framework by effectively leveraging \emph{auxiliary data}—samples of the source function of the heat equation—to design a \emph{physics-informed energy regularization}. Our analysis reveals that learning in linear parabolic PDEs exhibits intrinsic anisotropy between spatial and temporal regularity, in sharp contrast to the static elliptic problems, leading to fundamentally different estimation and generalization behaviors. Specifically, we derive non-asymptotically rate-optimal estimation errors, as well as generalization error, which explicitly capture the interplay among temporal sampling, spatial resolution, and solution smoothness. Our numerical experiments demonstrate substantial orders of magnitude of reduction in testing errors against various physics-informed neural network methods on various parabolic and hyperbolic PDEs.

Read more

entry.title: Enhancing Statistical-Computational Balance in Uncertainty Quantification of Bagging: A Cheap Bootstrap Approach

link.title: Enhancing Statistical-Computational Balance in Uncertainty Quantification of Bagging: A Cheap Bootstrap Approach

entry.content:
Bagging, which refers to the repeated subsampling of data and averaging the resulting outputs, is a common approach to reduce sampling variability of unstable learning and data-driven optimization procedures. However, uncertainty quantification for these bagged estimators, namely to generate confidence intervals for their target quantities, faces challenges in the simultaneous attainment of coverage validity while being computationally affordable. The latter refers to the practical consideration of overall resampling effort which, when using conventional bootstraps for instance, would lead to nested resampling procedures and thus can be multiplicatively large. In this paper, we develop an interval construction approach that is both asymptotically coverage-valid and computationally light in that it does not use much more than the resampling effort in the bagging scheme itself. Our approach builds on the recent so-called cheap bootstrap idea, a method designed to substantially reduce the number of resamples based on an integrative treatment between data noises and Monte Carlo resampling noises, and an in-depth derivation of the algorithmic configurations under which the Monte Carlo error from incomplete bagging is negligible. Our theory shows that our required computation budget is significantly smaller than existing methods in relation to the bag size and number of Monte Carlo subsamples. Numerical experiments in random forests, as well as an optimality bound estimation in stochastic optimization where bagging is useful, show that our proposed intervals achieve reliable coverage with low computation cost.

entry.title: Equilibrium Distribution for t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding with Generalized Kernels

link.title: Equilibrium Distribution for t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding with Generalized Kernels

entry.content:
We extend the results by Auffinger and Fletcher in 2023 on the large-sample limit of t-SNE to a broader class of input and output kernels. We prove that under natural assumptions on the input distribution and the decay of the output kernel, if perplexity scales linearly with data size, the empirical measures and values of minimizers converge to an equilibrium distribution. We conclude with numerical examples comparing different kernels.

entry.title: Equilibrium Learning in Unbounded Stochastic Games with Gaussian Transitions

link.title: Equilibrium Learning in Unbounded Stochastic Games with Gaussian Transitions

entry.content:
Learning equilibria from data is difficult when several decision makers interact indefinitely and the system state has no prescribed bounds. We examine discounted general-sum stochastic games with compact action sets and an unknown nonlinear drift observed through Gaussian transition noise. The proposed procedure uses a single uninterrupted trajectory to update Gaussian-process models of the drift and to solve successively refined finite games. We prove a perturbation result showing that stability of equilibrium selection, together with uniform KL accuracy of Gaussian transition models, is sufficient for regional uniform convergence of the induced values and approximate Nash behavior in the original game. The region specifies where the guarantees are evaluated; strategies and dynamics continue to act on the entire Euclidean state space. For GP estimators, simultaneous confidence bounds yield a rate controlled by posterior uncertainty, kernel information gain, and joint-state dimension. Numerical studies illustrate how kernel choice and dimension appear in the predicted convergence behavior.

Read more

entry.title: Estimating marginal association between paired outcomes in clustered data with an application to analyzing caries and periodontal disease data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey

link.title: Estimating marginal association between paired outcomes in clustered data with an application to analyzing caries and periodontal disease data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey

entry.content:
The within-cluster subgroup composition of units can inform on the marginal distribution of those units outcomes, denoted informative subgroup size (ISS). Moreover, within-cluster subgroup composition of paired outcomes can allow one outcome to inform upon the marginal distribution of the other. If this type of ISS ignored, it can bias marginal association estimates by allowing subgroup composition to influence how clusters contribute to the analysis. We develop two weighting approaches for estimating marginal association between paired outcomes in this setting. The weights are derived using within-cluster resampling arguments and extend conventional cluster weighting to paired response subgroups. We adapt an existing test of marginal dependence to assess ISS by examining this subgroup structure in both directions. In simulated data exhibiting this bidirectional ISS, pair-based weighting reduced bias when association was primarily carried through the paired observations. These weights also allow scientifically or clinically meaningful dichotomizations to enter directly into the weighting scheme, with the choice of subgroup definition further improving estimation in several simulated settings. Application to NHANES oral-health data showed strong evidence of ISS for filled-surface outcomes across subgroups defined by clinical attachment loss and pocket depth, with the corresponding periodontal–caries associations generally small and positive. These methods provide a practical approach for estimating marginal association when paired subgroup composition is informative.

Read more

entry.title: Estimation and Inference for Win Measures with Multiple Ordinal Endpoints Subject to Missingness

link.title: Estimation and Inference for Win Measures with Multiple Ordinal Endpoints Subject to Missingness

entry.content:
Win measures, including the win ratio, win odds, net benefit, and desirability of outcome ranking, are increasingly used in randomized clinical trials with multiple hierarchical ordinal endpoints. In practice, however, one or more component endpoints may have missing data. The standard pairwise-comparison approach, which treats pairs with missing outcomes as ties, can produce biased estimates, even if the data are missing completely at random. Although inverse probability of censoring weighting methods have been developed for censored survival endpoints, corresponding methods for addressing missing hierarchical ordinal endpoints are not yet available. To address this gap, we develop inverse probability weighted (IPW) and augmented IPW (AIPW) estimators for win measures with hierarchical ordinal endpoints subject to missing data, allowing missingness to depend on treatment assignment and baseline covariates. The IPW estimator corrects bias by reweighting complete observed outcomes using joint non-missingness probabilities involved in estimating the joint cell probabilities that define the win measures. The AIPW estimator additionally incorporates outcome modeling, potentially improving estimation precision and achieving double robustness. For inference, we derive closed-form variance estimators for both methods based on influence functions. Simulation studies show that the standard approach can be substantially biased, whereas the proposed IPW and AIPW estimators exhibit small bias and near-nominal coverage under their respective identifying and model conditions. Applications to the SCOUT-CAP and ACTT-1 trials illustrate the practical utility of the proposed methods. An R package WinMO is provided for implementation.

entry.title: Explaining Heterogeneous Treatment Effects with Causal Forests and the Hoeffding Functional Decomposition

link.title: Explaining Heterogeneous Treatment Effects with Causal Forests and the Hoeffding Functional Decomposition

entry.content:
The estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects is a central objective of causal inference. However, state-of-the-art algorithms to solve this task are based on machine learning principles, and thus behave as black boxes. Consequently, the identification of covariates driving heterogeneity remains a challenging and open problem. To address this limitation, we introduce CausalTreeHFD, an interpretable extension of causal forests, based on the Hoeffding functional decomposition adapted to tree ensembles. Our approach decomposes predictions of conditional average treatment effects (CATE) into contributions from individual covariates and pairwise interactions, providing a direct characterization of the factors driving treatment effect heterogeneity. We establish the consistency of CausalTreeHFD, which converges towards the Hoeffding decomposition of the underlying CATE function, under standard assumptions for the analysis of causal forests. Experiments on simulated and real datasets show that CausalTreeHFD accurately identifies relevant covariates and interactions, and precisely recovers their contributions to heterogeneous treatment effects.

Read more

entry.title: Exploration strategies for Gaussian process bandit optimization with inference regret guarantees

link.title: Exploration strategies for Gaussian process bandit optimization with inference regret guarantees

entry.content:
Existing cumulative regret guarantees for Bayesian optimization (BO) do not necessarily characterize the quality of the algorithm’s final output. This gap is critical under noisy evaluations, where the goal is to return a single high-quality recommendation. To address it, we introduce efficient exploration strategies that can be incorporated into any BO procedure by occasionally replacing the acquisition query with an exploration query. To validate this approach, we bound the Gaussian process posterior standard deviation over the search space via the fill distance of the queries, which measures the largest region left unexplored. We then use this result to derive upper bounds on the inference regret, i.e., the gap between the global optimum and the function value at the algorithm’s returned point. Empirically, these exploration strategies improve the final recommendations of existing BO algorithms on synthetic benchmarks, hyperparameter optimization, and a control task.

Read more

entry.title: Exploring Exchangeability within Permutation Inference: Implications for Statistics and Data Science Educators

link.title: Exploring Exchangeability within Permutation Inference: Implications for Statistics and Data Science Educators

entry.content:
Permutation tests are a powerful and flexible approach to inference via resampling. As computational methods become more ubiquitous in the statistics curriculum, use of permutation tests has become more tractable. At the heart of the permutation approach is the exchangeability condition, which determines the appropriate null sampling distribution. We explore the exchangeability condition in the context of permutation tests, including settings where the exchangeability condition is not tenable. Our examples include two-sample comparisons of means, clustered designs, multiple linear regression, and two-sample comparisons of correlation. The different exchangeability challenges in each example allow further exploration of the definition and importance of the exchangeability requirement for permutation testing. We believe that understanding the exchangeability condition and how it relates to the null hypothesis gives students the skills to work effectively with permutation tests in more complicated modeling settings and to further their understanding of statistical inference. We close with pedagogical recommendations for instructors who wish to incorporate permutation inference into their curriculum as a means to increase student understanding of resampling-based inference.

Read more
